summary.text: Hafnium research provides two very different antimicrobial examples: nanostructured oxide-coated surfaces and functionalized oxide nanoparticles. In the first, surface geometry is central; in the second, a targeting and polymeric formulation changes interaction with dental bacteria. Neither example supports treating bulk hafnium, dissolved ions, and engineered particles as interchangeable agents.

mechanisms.text: Boden and colleagues deposited hafnium through colloidal templates, producing surfaces whose measured outer chemistry was hafnium oxide. After 24 hours with S. aureus or E. coli, fluorescent staining revealed material- and organism-dependent membrane damage. Flat oxide films performed similarly to the control, while selected nanoscale patterns reduced attached-cell viability. No hafnium leaching was detected under the tested conditions, supporting a topography-related interpretation.

Ostadhossein and colleagues developed polymeric-silane-conjugated hafnium oxide nanoparticles with a peptide targeting S. mutans. They combined X-ray contrast with antibacterial testing, reported bacterial DNA fragmentation, and tested mature biofilms on extracted human teeth. The particles were also applied topically in a rodent dental-biofilm model over eight days. These are results for the assembled formulation, including its surface functionalization.

Another in vitro study sputtered hafnium oxide onto zirconia and titanium and measured S. mutans and P. gingivalis colonization together with pre-osteoblast responses. The coating reduced bacterial adhesion while supporting cell viability and differentiation in those assays. Its surface properties and organisms differed from the colloidal-template experiment, so the studies should not be collapsed into a universal claim about flat hafnium oxide.

microbiome.text: The coating experiments used separate bacterial species, not a mixed community. The dental work moved from an ex vivo human-tooth substrate to a living animal, but a rodent S. mutans challenge still does not establish selectivity or ecological benefit across the human oral microbiome. Diagnostic contrast and bacterial suppression are also separate performance measures.

exposure.text: Template size altered deposited-coating architecture, whereas topical delivery and targeting defined particle exposure. Sputtered dental coatings added another surface preparation. The dental particle study’s X-ray imaging capability should not be misread as a requirement for X-ray-activated bacterial killing.

limits.text: Membrane-compromised staining is an assay endpoint, not proof that a coating prevents clinical infection. The particle study provides preclinical evidence, not a human dental-treatment trial. Long-term coating durability, effects of a salivary conditioning layer, particle clearance, and host-tissue responses need their own assessment before these material concepts can be generalized.

summary.text: Tantalum highlights a distinction between killing bacteria directly and helping a host resist infection at an implant interface. Two preclinical studies reported favorable infection outcomes despite little or no intrinsic antibacterial advantage in isolated culture assays. Their proposed explanations involve host cells and local immunity, making the living tissue environment part of the material’s effect.

mechanisms.text: Chen and colleagues compared polished tantalum with titanium in an implant-associated tibial osteomyelitis model. Tantalum had a lower infectious state in vivo, but bacterial adhesion and antibacterial activity were not superior in vitro. In cell–bacteria–material experiments, fibroblasts attached more readily to tantalum; bacteria then associated with those cells, and later cell detachment removed attached bacteria. This was a proposed interface mechanism, not proof of direct bactericidal chemistry.

A different study deposited a tantalum nanofilm on titanium by magnetron sputtering. Infection models again showed activity without a direct culture-killing effect. Ex vivo experiments linked the coating to increased neutrophil phagocytosis, reduced neutrophil lysis, and altered macrophage cytokine release. The authors interpreted local innate immune support as contributing to bacterial control.

An independent study used equal-sized pieces from tantalum and titanium acetabular components. S. aureus and S. epidermidis grew on both, and washing, sonication, and further incubation did not reveal an antibiofilm advantage for tantalum. This negative result strengthens the need to separate intrinsic antibacterial action from infection outcomes in a living host.

microbiome.text: These studies do not measure a beneficial whole-microbiome change. Their microbial setting is an experimentally challenged implant or surrounding tissue. The useful ecological insight is that host-cell occupancy, immune activity, and bacterial attachment interact; a material’s behavior cannot always be reconstructed by exposing bacteria to a bare surface in isolation.

exposure.text: The interventions were polished tantalum and a deposited tantalum nanofilm, not soluble tantalum dosing. Surface preparation and the underlying substrate therefore belong in the exposure description. The nanofilm study measured biocompatibility within its experimental systems, but that observation cannot substitute for clinical follow-up across different implant designs.

limits.text: The lack of direct killing should remain visible beside positive animal findings. Differences between host-cell assays and infected tissue also mean that an explanatory mechanism requires further testing. These results do not show that every tantalum implant prevents infection or that stimulating an inflammatory response is uniformly beneficial in every tissue context.

summary.text: Rhenium compounds show why coordination structure and activation conditions must accompany any antimicrobial claim. Closely related carbonyl complexes can be inactive or active, and illumination can change the bacterial spectrum. The evidence includes chemical screens, computational target hypotheses, and carefully controlled light-versus-dark susceptibility assays. It does not establish an antimicrobial property of elemental rhenium.

mechanisms.text: Schindler and colleagues screened rhenium di- and tricarbonyl diimine compounds against eight microorganisms. The tested dicarbonyl compounds and neutral tricarbonyl species lacked bactericidal or bacteriostatic activity. Computational comparisons suggested the S. aureus membrane proteins LtaA and LspA as possible binding partners for active molecules. Docking is a prioritization tool here; the study did not establish direct engagement of those proteins in bacterial cells.

Frei and colleagues tested a different rhenium complex series with and without 365 nm irradiation for one hour, approximately 3 J/cm². S. aureus responded in both conditions, with stronger activity under light. E. coli lacked detectable dark susceptibility at the tested concentrations but became susceptible after irradiation. Uptake and mutant experiments implicated efflux as a barrier to the light-independent effect.

A 2026 mercaptopyrimidine complex series added explicit solution-stability work. ReB4 inhibited S. aureus, including resistant strains, and showed a biofilm-inhibition endpoint; other members gradually decomposed in water. This reinforces that nominally similar rhenium molecules may change during an assay and that starting composition is not always the final exposure.

microbiome.text: These are defined culture systems, not intact microbiomes. Biofilm inhibition in the newer study should not be called eradication of an established biofilm. Docked protein targets, light-dependent susceptibility, and aqueous instability belong to different compound series rather than one proven rhenium mechanism.

exposure.text: The photochemical lead became more toxic to human kidney-derived cells after irradiation, making light delivery part of the safety assessment. In the newer series, ligand exchange and decomposition changed aqueous behavior. Both observations argue for measuring the biologically encountered species and conditions.

limits.text: An active charged compound and an inactive neutral analogue do not isolate charge as the sole causal feature. Docking supplies hypotheses, while a culture selectivity ratio supplies neither pharmacokinetics nor human efficacy. Light delivery and solution stability each require independent validation before the corresponding system can advance.

summary.text: Osmium antimicrobial research spans growth-inhibitory organometallic complexes and a light-activated composite material. These interventions differ in ligand structure, delivery, and mechanism. The most useful evidence combines positive bacterial findings with explicit mammalian-cell comparisons: high potency alone does not establish a clinically useful therapeutic margin.

mechanisms.text: In glycosyl-heterocyclic half-sandwich compounds, quinoline-containing osmium and ruthenium complexes inhibited resistant Gram-positive isolates. Changing carbohydrate protecting groups or the heterocycle altered biological activity. These compounds were also investigated for cancer-cell cytostasis, making the distinction between bacterial inhibition and general cellular activity especially important.

A separate screen of 17 osmium–arene complexes against Mycobacterium tuberculosis identified potent iodido compounds. Potency patterns resembled those measured in normal human lung cells. Osmium uptake from the lead compound was rapid and temperature-dependent, consistent with an active-transport contribution. The authors proposed a thiol-related redox mechanism; this remains an interpretation rather than a uniquely verified bacterial target.

A 2025 study incorporated an osmium polypyridyl complex into a UiO-67-bpy framework and used 800–810 nm near-infrared light. Its selected composite increased reactive-oxygen-species generation and reduced S. aureus and E. coli viability. The illuminated formulation also improved wound-healing outcomes in a mouse S. aureus challenge. The active intervention was a composite plus light, not the isolated metal.

microbiome.text: The resistant Gram-positive isolates, M. tuberculosis cultures, and mouse wound challenge answer different questions. None establishes benefit to an intact human microbiome. In particular, inhibition of planktonic organisms should not be assumed to eradicate a mature biofilm or remove all bacteria from an infected wound.

exposure.text: The glycosyl compounds and osmium–arene candidates were chemically defined molecules tested in culture. The framework study added carrier composition and light delivery as determinants of exposure. Its cell-toxicity and hemolysis measurements were limited assay results; they do not establish systemic safety or the fate of a retained metal-containing material.

limits.text: The tuberculosis study is a caution against treating activity as selectivity: bacterial and normal-cell potency moved together. The near-infrared system supplies an animal result, but short-term wound recovery does not demonstrate human efficacy, sterilization, or freedom from delayed toxicity. Each formulation needs its own pharmacological and ecological assessment.

summary.text: Iridium complexes are being developed for several distinct antibacterial strategies, including extracellular-DNA disruption, light-driven oxidation, and direct growth inhibition. Their ligands and physical conditions define the intervention. A biofilm-active compound, an imaging photosensitizer, and an anti-staphylococcal diamine complex cannot be treated as interchangeable evidence about iridium.

mechanisms.text: Li and colleagues designed four cyclometalated Ir(III) compounds and identified Ir2 as the most active in their series. The study linked Gram-positive targeting to lipoteichoic-acid interactions and reported membrane damage, genomic-DNA damage, and degradation of biofilm extracellular DNA. This last endpoint addresses a structural biofilm component rather than only the growth of freely suspended cells.

Ho and colleagues developed cationic cyclometalated complexes that fluoresce when associated with bacteria and generate reactive oxygen species under illumination. Two closely related structural isomers generated similar ROS signals in buffer but differed in bacterial photoinactivation. Thus, solution photochemistry alone did not predict biological performance; interaction with the bacterial envelope also mattered.

Karpin and colleagues tested a different family of cyclopentadienyl metal–diamine complexes against S. aureus and patient MRSA isolates. A cis-diaminocyclohexane iridium compound had a reported MIC of 4 μg/mL and MBC of 8 μg/mL. Ligand methylation reduced activity. The investigators also screened hemolysis and Vero-cell toxicity, providing useful but limited host-cell context.

microbiome.text: Ir2 was tested topically in a mouse S. aureus biofilm-infected wound model, extending the work beyond culture assays. Its animal result remains distinct from a human wound trial or evidence of beneficial microbiome restructuring. The fluorescence study showed interactions with both Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms but did not establish a community-wide therapeutic effect.

exposure.text: The imaging study used white-light irradiation; its microscopy comparison specified 134 mW/cm² for 30 minutes. That condition belongs to the photodynamic system and must not be imported into the separate Ir2 wound study. Likewise, a minimum inhibitory concentration for one diamine compound cannot be assigned to another iridium scaffold.

limits.text: DNA damage can be useful against bacteria but makes host selectivity a central question. A negative hemolysis or Vero-cell assay does not establish long-term tissue safety. Biofilm penetration, removal of viable cells, damage to extracellular matrix, and wound healing should remain separate endpoints when evaluating any lead compound.

summary.text: Bismuth links antimicrobial metallomics to direct metal substitution and broader metabolic disruption. The clearest molecular example is displacement of zinc from bacterial metallo-β-lactamases. Work in Helicobacter pylori, however, shows that bismuth drugs can affect many proteins and pathways. A single substituted metal site is therefore not a universal explanation for every bismuth-sensitive bacterium.

mechanisms.text: Wang and colleagues used structural and functional experiments to show that one Bi(III) ion could displace two Zn(II) ions from tested metallo-β-lactamases. These enzymes otherwise hydrolyze important β-lactam antibiotics. Colloidal bismuth subcitrate restored meropenem activity against MBL-positive bacteria in vitro and in a mouse infection model, supporting a drug-repurposing hypothesis rather than a demonstrated clinical combination therapy.

In H. pylori, integrated metalloproteomics and quantitative proteomics identified 63 bismuth-binding and 119 bismuth-regulated proteins. Functional assays implicated several systems, including oxidative-stress defense and pH buffering. DnaK was investigated as a possible link to impaired attachment to host cells. Binding, altered abundance, and functional inhibition are complementary observations; none should be substituted automatically for another.

A time-resolved transcriptomic and metabolomic study followed the response to a bismuth drug. The authors observed early perturbation of central carbon metabolism, followed by effects on urease, oxidative stress, and energy production. The timing offers a way to distinguish early responses from later cellular deterioration, while still leaving the causal hierarchy of individual targets open to testing.

microbiome.text: These studies focus on pathogens and their molecular responses. They do not establish a favorable change in total human gut-community composition. An H. pylori enzyme or adhesion result also cannot be transferred directly to a different organism expressing a zinc-dependent resistance enzyme; the bacteria, target proteins, and treatment combinations differ.

exposure.text: The experiments used specified Bi(III) compounds, including colloidal bismuth subcitrate. Chemical formulation, bacterial uptake, and the presence of an antibiotic partner define the exposure. A result from this drug cannot be assigned to elemental bismuth, every bismuth salt, or a nanoparticle simply because all contain the same element.

limits.text: The enzyme study supplies unusually direct structural evidence for mismetallation, but clinical usefulness still depends on delivery and selectivity in a host. Proteome-wide response measurements identify candidate mechanisms; essentiality, target occupancy, and the contribution of each pathway require additional experiments. Established use of a bismuth formulation in one indication does not validate every proposed combination or dose.

summary.text: Scandium can alter bacterial gene expression and the production of extracellular enzymes and secondary metabolites. It is a rare-earth element, but not a lanthanide. The evidence here concerns a culture condition that changes microbial behavior, rather than an established scandium-containing enzyme or a universal nutritional requirement.

mechanisms.text: In Bacillus subtilis, scandium addition stimulated production of amylase and the antimicrobial metabolite bacilysin. Transcriptional measurements linked the response to increased expression of the relevant genes, distinguishing it from simply adding a metal to an already purified enzyme.

In Streptomyces coelicolor A3(2), scandium and/or lanthanum increased expression of genes from multiple secondary-metabolite biosynthetic clusters. Chemical profiling detected compounds in treated cultures that were not detected under the untreated conditions.

microbiome.text: Both studies used bacterial isolates. Inducing a metabolite in a flask does not establish a beneficial effect in a human microbial community, nor show that the same genes are expressed in soil. Production, secretion, ecological activity, and host benefit are different endpoints.

exposure.text: The experiments supplied rare-earth compounds in growth media, making concentration and medium composition integral to the result. An observed low-concentration response should not be interpreted as evidence that increasing scandium indefinitely would continue to improve production.

limits.text: Gene induction can help researchers uncover otherwise poorly expressed biosynthetic capacity, but it does not by itself identify a metabolite’s structure or activity. The experiments also do not establish that scandium is the direct signal, a catalytic cofactor, or an indirect source of cellular stress in every responding organism.

summary.text: Yttrium has direct microbial evidence for biosorption and for recognition by a selective metal-binding protein. Neither observation establishes that bacteria require yttrium for growth. Although grouped with the rare-earth elements, yttrium is not a lanthanide, and its biology should be evaluated on its own evidence.

mechanisms.text: Serratia marcescens biomass bound yttrium from experimental wastewater. Spectroscopic analyses implicated hydroxyl, carboxyl, and amino groups, with the results consistent with ion exchange, electrostatic interactions, and complexation at the biomass surface.

The bacterial protein lanmodulin responded strongly to Y(III) as well as trivalent lanthanides. Its metal-dependent structural change occurred at much lower metal concentrations than its response to calcium. Recognition by this protein is a binding result, not proof that yttrium performs the catalytic job of a lanthanide.

microbiome.text: The evidence concerns an engineered wastewater-treatment assay and purified bacterial protein. Neither study examined a human microbiome. For community ecology, the unresolved question is whether selective binding changes metal availability to neighboring organisms.

exposure.text: Yttrium sorption varied with pH, starting metal concentration, biomass dose, contact time, mixing, and temperature. The reported capacity is conditional on the optimized laboratory system; it should not be treated as a universal property of the species or of untreated industrial wastewater.

limits.text: Removal from water transfers yttrium into another fraction; it does not destroy the element. A recovery process must consider release, competing ions, and handling of metal-bearing biomass. Protein selectivity likewise does not establish intact-cell uptake or a yttrium nutritional requirement.

summary.text: Lanthanum is a functional cofactor in selected bacterial alcohol dehydrogenases. Its importance extends beyond fitting a metal into an enzyme: cells must recognize, acquire, transport, and store the ion. The best-characterized systems are specialized environmental bacteria, and their requirements do not imply a lanthanum requirement for people or for every microbiome.

mechanisms.text: ExaF from Methylobacterium extorquens AM1 preferentially incorporated La(III) when calcium was also available. With its PQQ cofactor, the purified enzyme oxidized ethanol and also acted on several other alcohol or aldehyde substrates. This extended lanthanide biochemistry beyond methanol oxidation alone.

Lanmodulin illustrates selective recognition: a bacterial protein can respond to trivalent lanthanides at concentrations far below those needed for a calcium response. Binding selectivity is an important upstream property, but it is distinct from the enzyme activity that eventually supports metabolism.

Mutant and uptake studies in Methylorubrum extorquens AM1 implicated a TonB–ABC transport system in lanthanide incorporation into the cytoplasm. Microscopy showed intracellular metal-rich inclusions resembling polyphosphate granules, adding storage to the acquisition pathway.

microbiome.text: The cited work concerns cultured methylotrophic bacteria and purified proteins. It does not establish the prevalence of lanthanum-dependent activity in human gut communities. Even within a cultured organism, alternative enzymes can make a pathway useful without making one enzyme absolutely necessary for growth.

exposure.text: Soluble La(III) added to defined medium is readily accessible compared with many environmental mineral sources. Uptake regulation and intracellular sequestration help explain why supplying a metal and detecting total cell-associated metal are not the same as measuring delivery to the active enzyme.

limits.text: ExaF deletion did not abolish ethanol growth in the original study, despite its biochemical contribution to ethanol metabolism. That distinction matters: activity in an enzyme assay, contribution in a cell, and essentiality of an entire organism are progressively stronger claims.

summary.text: Cerium has a well-defined role in the methanol-oxidizing machinery of selected bacteria and a separate documented effect on extracellular polymer production. Its biological interpretation depends on chemical form: dissolved Ce(III) in culture is not interchangeable with cerium-oxide nanoparticles or other cerium-containing materials.

mechanisms.text: The acidophilic methanotroph Methylacidiphilum fumariolicum SolV required lanthanides for growth. Protein purification and crystallography linked that dependence to a lanthanide-containing XoxF methanol dehydrogenase, with cerium serving as an enzyme metal. This reaction handles methanol produced during methane oxidation.

A soil Bradyrhizobium isolate formed abundant extracellular polysaccharide when grown with CeCl3. Chemical analysis identified a predominantly rhamnose-based polymer. Other tested light lanthanides could also trigger the response, but heavier members did not behave uniformly.

microbiome.text: The methane-oxidizing organism originated in a volcanic mudpot; the polymer-producing bacterium was a soil isolate. These observations concern environmental metabolism and culture phenotypes, not a demonstrated cerium-dependent human gut function or a human microbiome benefit.

exposure.text: The growth and enzyme experiments focus on available trivalent ions. The polysaccharide screen used 30 micromolar CeCl3 on a specified dilute nutrient medium. Both the ligand environment and the growth medium matter when comparing such results with particles, minerals, or environmental total-cerium measurements.

limits.text: A polymer-production response does not prove that cerium is incorporated as a cofactor in its biosynthesis. Nor does XoxF activity establish that every methanotroph requires cerium specifically: the reported organism could use several lanthanides. Responses must be assigned to the tested strain and metal form.

summary.text: Praseodymium has direct experimental support as a usable metal in bacterial alcohol oxidation. Evidence comes from a nonmethylotrophic soil bacterium and from comparative studies of methylotrophs. This is an element-specific experimental role, rather than an inference based only on the better-known lanthanum and cerium examples.

mechanisms.text: Purified PedH from Pseudomonas putida KT2440 was active with Pr(III), as well as several other light lanthanides. Its calcium-dependent counterpart, PedE, acts on overlapping alcohol and aldehyde substrates. The two systems allow the bacterium to respond to different metal environments.

Comparative growth tests with Methylotenera mobilis and Methylomonas sp. included praseodymium among growth-supporting light lanthanides. Different XoxF enzyme types accepted different ranges of the series, showing why a result for one lanthanide or one enzyme cannot define all the others.

microbiome.text: These are environmental isolates and enzyme systems, not human microbiome experiments. The most immediate ecological question is how metal availability influences use of alcohol substrates and competition among environmental bacteria.

exposure.text: Pr(III) supplied in a defined medium is the relevant experimental species. Purified-enzyme activity, whole-cell growth, and regulation were measured with different assays; in particular, a regulatory threshold established with lanthanum should not be relabeled as a praseodymium threshold.

limits.text: PedH activity confirms a biochemical capability but not an exclusive need for praseodymium. The comparative XoxF work also warns that artificial electron-acceptor assays do not fully reconstruct the natural electron-transfer chain. Metal preference may differ between an isolated enzyme and a living community.

summary.text: Neodymium connects enzyme structure, metal preference, and mineral acquisition in microbial metallomics. It has been directly identified in an active methanol dehydrogenase, yet not every lanthanide-using bacterium prefers it. Work comparing soluble and poorly soluble neodymium sources also reveals how microbes obtain the metal before using it.

mechanisms.text: XoxF1 purified from Methylacidimicrobium thermophilum AP8 contained neodymium after growth with it as the sole supplied lanthanide. Metal measurements, X-ray crystallography, and kinetic assays tied Nd to a functional methanol-oxidizing active site.

Methylorubrum extorquens AM1 favored lanthanum when both La and Nd were supplied. Purified XoxF from mixed-metal cultures contained more lanthanum, and La-loaded enzyme had greater activity and thermal stability than Nd-loaded enzyme. Similar chemistry does not mean identical biological performance.

A 2024 study compared soluble NdCl3 with poorly soluble Nd2O3 in Methylobacterium extorquens AM1. It identified methylolanthanin, a small secreted metal-binding molecule. Disrupting its biosynthetic genes impaired normal metal accumulation, whereas overexpression increased accumulation and adsorption.

microbiome.text: These experiments involve environmental methane- or methanol-utilizing bacteria. They do not establish a neodymium role in human intestinal communities. They do demonstrate that “bioavailable neodymium” is a biological as well as a chemical question, because cells can modify their acquisition machinery.

exposure.text: The AP8 work supplied neodymium to acidic growth medium; the acquisition study deliberately compared a chloride salt with an oxide. Chemical form, pH, ligands, and alternative lanthanides determine the relevance of a total-neodymium measurement.

limits.text: A crystallographically observed metal establishes an active-site assignment, not universal essentiality. The comparison with lanthanum was made in a different enzyme and organism from AP8. Those results are complementary examples of specificity, not conflicting estimates of one universal neodymium preference.

summary.text: Gadolinium illustrates three different microbial outcomes: use after laboratory adaptation, binding to microbial biomass, and cellular stress in yeast. These should not be conflated. A bacterium able to grow with gadolinium has a particular physiological solution; it does not demonstrate a general nutrient role or a beneficial effect in a host microbiome.

mechanisms.text: An evolved Methylorubrum extorquens AM1 variant grew on methanol with gadolinium. A regulatory mutation produced broad changes in gene expression and increased accumulation into an intracellular compartment described as a lanthasome. The experiment shows that accessible metal use can change through adaptation.

A comparison of bacterial and yeast biomass found marked differences in Gd(III) sorption, with effects of growth stage and medium composition. Binding by biomass is a physicochemical endpoint and does not require demonstration of gadolinium-dependent energy metabolism.

A Saccharomyces cerevisiae deletion screen identified genes whose loss increased sensitivity or resistance to gadolinium nitrate. Calcium signaling, phosphate metabolism, and vesicle transport were among the implicated processes. Sensitive mutants also accumulated more intracellular gadolinium.

microbiome.text: The yeast screen measures a microbial eukaryote’s response; the evolved bacterial strain measures an acquired growth capability. Neither tests a human gut community. Across these models, the same element can be bound, compartmentalized, or toxic without those outcomes being mutually exclusive.

exposure.text: The evolved strain could acquire gadolinium from gadopentetic acid in culture. That result concerns one chelated compound in a bacterial system. It cannot be applied automatically to other chelates, contrast-agent behavior inside a person, or free Gd(III) exposure.

limits.text: A gene-deletion phenotype identifies a process that affects susceptibility, not necessarily a direct metal target. Sorption results also depend on how cells were grown and prepared. The studies support several testable mechanisms but not the use of these microbes to treat exposure.

name: Other lanthanides
role: Comparative enzyme chemistry and evidence gaps

summary.text: Samarium, europium, terbium, dysprosium, holmium, erbium, thulium, ytterbium, and lutetium belong in the atlas, but their evidence is uneven. Comparative enzyme assays cover the series; europium also has direct structural and growth evidence, and samarium has experimental biomineralization evidence. No single “rare-earth effect” should be assigned to every member.

mechanisms.text: A methanol dehydrogenase from Methylacidiphilum fumariolicum SolV was tested with lanthanides from La to Lu, excluding radioactive promethium. Earlier members supported higher activity than later ones. The study combined kinetic assays with calculations to investigate consequences of decreasing ionic size across the series.

SolV grown with europium yielded an enzyme with Eu in its active site. The overall protein structure remained similar to previously characterized forms, but catalytic efficiency was lower. Europium-supported growth and an isolated active enzyme are stronger evidence than metal binding alone.

In separate samarium experiments, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Pseudomonas fluorescens, and Bacillus subtilis first adsorbed Sm and subsequently developed samarium-phosphate particles on their surfaces. Mineral formation occurred more rapidly at higher pH within the tested acidic range.

microbiome.text: These studies concern environmental microbial cultures, cell surfaces, and purified enzymes. They do not establish individual human microbiome functions for the listed elements. For Tb, Dy, Ho, Er, Tm, Yb, and Lu, the evidence highlighted here remains comparative enzyme behavior, not a shared requirement for growth.

exposure.text: Trivalent ions in an enzyme assay differ from mineral-bound metals. In the samarium study, changing pH altered the timing of surface mineral formation. In the europium study, the growth medium and enzyme preparation were controlled to determine the active-site assignment.

limits.text: Series membership is not a substitute for direct measurement. A metal can bind a protein without supporting efficient catalysis, and catalysis in vitro does not guarantee uptake or growth. Promethium was not tested in the comparative work and is not assigned a microbial role by analogy.

summary.text: Strontium illustrates how microbial activity changes a mineral habitat. Urea-degrading bacteria can drive carbonate precipitation that captures dissolved Sr. The useful process is mineral formation: the element is transferred from water into a solid rather than consumed or destroyed.

mechanisms.text: Ureolysis changes solution chemistry and promotes calcium carbonate precipitation. In artificial groundwater, the rate of mineral growth and incubation temperature affected how Sr entered calcite. A single removal percentage therefore cannot describe every aquifer.

The salt-tolerant marine isolate Bacillus sp. TK2d showed a changing sequence of Sr association: early cellular and surface interactions preceded extensive incorporation into extracellular carbonate minerals.

microbiome.text: The strongest evidence here comes from isolates and controlled water chemistry. It does not establish that a natural soil community will precipitate the same minerals at the same rate. Temperature and precipitation kinetics provide a concrete bridge between microbial metabolism and the final geochemical outcome.

exposure.text: The TK2d study addressed saline conditions, where competing ions complicate capture. Experiments with dissolved Sr inform possible radionuclide immobilization, but stable Sr capture is not itself a demonstration of radiological cleanup. The identity and persistence of the solid matter as much as the decline in dissolved concentration.

limits.text: Batch mineralization establishes a mechanism, not long-term containment. Extrapolating to groundwater requires accounting for flow, competing ions, mineral dissolution, and the consequences of the chemistry used to stimulate precipitation. Those are deployment questions beyond a controlled ureolysis experiment.

summary.text: Technetium connects microbial electron transfer to radionuclide mobility. Dissolved Tc(VII), commonly studied as pertechnetate, can be reduced to less soluble Tc(IV). Microbes may catalyze that change directly or generate iron minerals that do the reducing chemistry outside the cell.

mechanisms.text: Geobacter sulfurreducens reduced Tc(VII) directly with hydrogen as electron donor. Acetate was much less effective in the direct reaction, although it supported an indirect route through microbial Fe(III) reduction.
Biogenic Fe(II), including Fe(II) in magnetite, can reduce technetium without an enzyme contacting every Tc ion. A microbial community may therefore control Tc fate through its effects on iron.
Sediment microcosms removed dissolved Tc during the development of iron-reducing conditions; spectroscopic measurements supported formation of hydrous Tc(IV) oxide.

microbiome.text: Community experiments add a layer that pure cultures cannot supply: several electron-accepting processes occur in succession as sediments become anoxic. Tc removal before sulfate reduction in one study shows why the stage of community metabolism matters, rather than simply whether microbes are present.

exposure.text: Oxidation state and subsequent oxygen exposure are central. In aquifer sediments, much of previously immobilized Tc was remobilized by air, while nitrate exposure caused little release in the tested systems. Oxidation of the surrounding iron did not translate automatically into the same Tc response.

limits.text: Reduction does not eliminate radioactivity, and initial removal from water is not proof of lasting isolation. Spectroscopy performed at elevated Tc concentrations can identify products, but its conditions should be distinguished from parallel experiments at trace concentrations.

summary.text: Palladium is a useful example of microbial metal recovery. Bacteria can reduce soluble Pd(II) to elemental Pd(0), forming particles associated with biomass. The reaction links metabolism to materials synthesis, but it does not mean palladium is a nutrient or that every palladium compound behaves alike.

mechanisms.text: Resting Desulfovibrio desulfuricans cells produced cell-associated Pd(0) with hydrogen, formate, or pyruvate as electron donor. The work established a biological route for recovering elemental palladium from solution.

In Shewanella oneidensis, pyruvate accelerated palladium reduction relative to lactate. Changes in catabolism and electron-transfer pathways connected the choice of substrate to the reduction process.

microbiome.text: These controlled bacterial experiments show that physiology and electron donors change palladium processing. They do not demonstrate beneficial effects on a human microbiome.

exposure.text: The studies begin with dissolved palladium species and end with particulate metal. Dissolved concentration, particle formation, and viable biomass are different measurements. Reporting only disappearance from solution cannot describe where the palladium went or what kind of recoverable material formed.

limits.text: Laboratory reduction does not establish palladium-supported growth, clinical efficacy, or reliable recovery from mixed waste. Catalytic performance of the particles needs separate measurement.

summary.text: Acid-producing microbial communities can release indium from discarded displays. They create a leaching environment; the evidence does not imply an indium-dependent metabolism or nutritional requirement.

mechanisms.text: Acidophilic bacteria process sulfur and iron substrates that change the chemistry around shredded displays. In a comparison of LCD leaching systems, sulfur-mediated communities achieved much greater indium release than the iron-mediated community.
Adaptation of Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans to waste OLED material, together with adjustments to pH, substrate supply, and solids loading, improved extraction in laboratory experiments.

microbiome.text: The LCD study followed community composition as well as extraction. Acidithiobacillus dominated the sulfur-mediated system. That gives a biological context to the leaching chemistry, while leaving open how much each community member contributed to acid generation or tolerance of the waste.

exposure.text: Indium bound in a display coating is not equivalent to a soluble indium salt. Waste preparation, acidity, the amount of solid material, and the presence of other elements determine accessibility. The OLED work recovered different metals with very different efficiencies, illustrating why “metal removal” is too broad a description.

limits.text: Batch extraction is not a complete recycling process. Selective recovery, reagent demands, residual solids, and variable waste feeds remain separate questions. Human microbiome effects were not tested.

summary.text: Cesium uptake can overlap with potassium transport, while resistance may depend on maintaining other intracellular ions. Uptake, tolerance, and useful environmental capture are distinct outcomes.

mechanisms.text: Bacteria from a soil conditioner showed saturable cesium uptake that potassium competitively inhibited. This supports a shared transport route rather than a dedicated biological demand for cesium.
In the cesium-resistant isolate Microbacterium sp. TS-1, genetic analysis implicated the magnesium transporter MgtE in resistance. Magnesium supply helped cells withstand cesium stress.

microbiome.text: The soil-conditioner experiment concerns environmental bacteria under controlled uptake conditions. In a mixed environment, potassium availability could change cesium entry even if community membership stays constant. This is a transport-level mechanism; it does not demonstrate that adding a bacterial product decontaminates field soil.

exposure.text: The TS-1 experiments used high cesium concentrations, unlike trace radiocesium in natural waters. Survival under this stress does not establish useful capture: resistant cells may exclude or export cesium.

limits.text: Neither potassium competition nor cesium resistance is sufficient evidence for a field-ready remediation process. A useful system must retain the isotope, permit collection of the contaminated biomass or product, and remain effective in realistic water chemistry. The cited studies do not establish those outcomes.

summary.text: Marine bacteria and extracellular polymers can concentrate barium and promote barite formation. A sponge symbiont also mineralizes barium internally, demonstrating a distinct host-associated route.

mechanisms.text: Extracellular polymeric substances, the material surrounding cells in biofilms, can bind Ba and concentrate it locally. Experiments identified an initially phosphorus-rich phase that developed into barite.

Mediterranean seawater isolates belonging to Pseudoalteromonas, Idiomarina, and Alteromonas formed barite in culture. Mineral production was associated with bacterial polymers and changed during maturation.

In the sponge Theonella swinhoei, the symbiont Entotheonella mineralized barium and arsenic on intracellular vesicles. This places mineral sequestration inside a host-associated bacterium rather than only on a biofilm surface.

microbiome.text: The sponge findings suggest a potential contribution to host metal handling, but localization of minerals does not by itself prove a benefit to sponge survival. The seawater experiments address a different scale: microbial processes that may contribute to the marine barium cycle and to interpretation of sedimentary Ba as a productivity proxy.

exposure.text: Dissolved barium and barium incorporated into sulfate minerals have different environmental behavior. Local concentration within a biofilm can favor mineral formation even when the surrounding water does not appear favorable. Bulk-water measurements may therefore miss the chemical conditions immediately around cells.

limits.text: Laboratory precipitation and microscopic localization establish pathways, not their global contributions to marine barite. Mineral accumulation also does not establish that a cell or host avoids metal stress.

summary.text: Platinum profiles need to separate microbial reduction, resistance, and engineered recovery. Fungi and bacteria can convert soluble platinum species into particles, while resistant cells can alter their physiology under exposure. None of these observations makes platinum an ordinary microbial cofactor.

mechanisms.text: Work with Fusarium oxysporum proposed a two-stage reduction pathway from Pt(IV) through Pt(II) to Pt(0), with different favorable conditions for the stages. It is a mechanistic model for a particular biological system.

In Citrobacter freundii JH, electron-transfer analysis implicated formate dehydrogenases, hydrogenases, and flavin-associated processes. Biogenic palladium promoted platinum reduction, linking two metals within the same electron-transfer system.
Engineered yeast displaying a hydrogenase produced elemental platinum particles from Pt(II). Microscopy and chemical analysis supported the identity of the recovered material.

microbiome.text: Laboratory evolution of Cupriavidus metallidurans produced increased platinum resistance alongside genomic and transcriptomic changes, including membrane-related responses. Such adaptation illustrates how exposure selects cellular traits; it is not evidence that platinum benefits a diverse environmental or host microbiome.

exposure.text: Pt(IV) salts, Pt(II) complexes, and elemental particles differ in accessibility and reaction pathway. The reduction bottleneck may change with oxidation state and electron supply. Conclusions from one dissolved salt cannot be assigned to all platinum materials or to a platinum-containing drug.

limits.text: Particle synthesis does not establish environmental persistence, catalytic performance, or clinical safety. Likewise, mutations found in a resistant lineage require additional functional work before each can be called a causal resistance mechanism. Recovery and tolerance should be evaluated with separate measurements.

summary.text: Gold is biologically active when encountered as soluble complexes, even though bulk metallic gold appears inert. Gold-associated bacteria can convert those complexes into less accessible forms. Their chemistry connects detoxification, extracellular molecules, and the formation of elemental gold.

mechanisms.text: Delftia acidovorans produces delftibactin, a secreted metallophore involved in gold biomineralization and protection against soluble gold. The protective chemistry can occur outside the cell.
In Cupriavidus metallidurans, gold and copper handling intersect. Gold complexes interfere with the CupA copper-export pathway, making mixed-metal exposure different from either metal alone.

The periplasmic copper oxidase CopA also acts in gold chemistry. Its activity helps limit cytoplasmic exposure to problematic gold species while contributing to conditions that favor periplasmic gold biomineralization. CopA and the exporter CupA are different proteins.

microbiome.text: These studies concern bacteria associated with gold-rich environments and laboratory mechanistic experiments. They show different ways organisms can manage soluble gold stress, not a universal gold pathway across microbes. Community-level consequences require measurements beyond the ability of an isolate to form gold particles.

exposure.text: Soluble gold complexes, elemental deposits, and formulated nanoparticles are distinct exposures. Delftibactin-mediated precipitation illustrates how a bacterium changes local exposure chemistry before gold reaches cellular targets.

limits.text: The cited mechanisms do not establish health benefits of gold exposure, probiotic gold detoxification, or safe environmental release of gold compounds. They also caution against predicting a metal response from a single-metal experiment when shared copper machinery is involved.

summary.text: Thorium can be sequestered by bacterial biomass and can alter biofilm communities. These are separate chemical and ecological findings.

mechanisms.text: Microscopy and elemental analysis located thorium within a Pseudomonas isolate, including intracellular precipitates; the study did not demonstrate thorium respiration.

Spectroscopy implicated phosphate, carboxyl, and amide groups, while diffraction identified crystalline thorium phosphate. Ion exchange, complexation, and microprecipitation can jointly explain sequestration.

microbiome.text: River-derived biofilms on ceramic plates were exposed in laboratory channels for four weeks. Thorium changed bacterial composition and diatom diversity and density; micromeiofauna did not show the same pattern. Different biological groups responded differently.

exposure.text: Thorium was measured in the experimental water. Because it binds to surfaces, the available exposure can differ from the amount initially added.

limits.text: Sequestration is not evidence of a nutritional requirement. The channel experiment demonstrates ecological effects under its conditions, not a universal toxicity threshold or human microbiome mechanism.

summary.text: Some metal-reducing bacteria conserve energy while converting soluble U(VI) into less soluble U(IV). This respiratory process can immobilize uranium, but its effectiveness depends on the organisms and surrounding geochemistry.

mechanisms.text: The early uranium-reduction work established that Fe(III)-reducing microorganisms could conserve energy while reducing uranium. This distinguishes a metabolic electron-accepting process from passive attachment to cell surfaces.

A separate Pseudomonas study found uranium and thorium sequestration associated with cellular binding groups and phosphate products. Its evidence illustrates why “biosorption” and “respiration” should not be used as synonyms.

At a contaminated aquifer in Rifle, Colorado, acetate addition stimulated indigenous Geobacter populations and coincided with declining dissolved uranium. The field response connected community activity with groundwater chemistry.

microbiome.text: The Rifle experiment also exposed a limit: as treatment continued and sulfate reducers became dominant, uranium removal weakened and dissolved concentrations rose. Supplying an electron donor did not guarantee that the community would keep performing the desired reaction indefinitely.

exposure.text: Oxidation state, ligands, and solid-product identity affect uranium mobility. Reduction changes chemical behavior and location; it does not convert the isotope into a nonradioactive element.

limits.text: A successful initial reduction phase is not proof of permanent groundwater protection. The field results make community succession a practical concern: the organisms favored early in treatment may lose prominence as electron acceptors and geochemistry change.

summary.text: Microbial Np(V) reduction and removal from water are distinct achievements. Mineral partners and phosphate chemistry influence whether reduced neptunium becomes effectively immobilized.

mechanisms.text: Shewanella putrefaciens reduced Np(V) in a controlled study, but reduction alone did not produce effective removal under the tested conditions. Coupling the process to phosphate release by Citrobacter supplied an additional route to precipitation.
In sediment microcosms amended with manganese oxide, microbial Mn reduction coincided with enhanced removal of dissolved Np and formation of Np(IV), supported by X-ray absorption spectroscopy.

microbiome.text: The sediment-community experiment linked neptunium behavior to manganese reduction, a stage preceding iron reduction. Enzymatic processes were considered potentially important, but the reaction was not assigned to a single enzyme.

exposure.text: The studies compare dissolved Np(V) with reduced and retained products. Chemical ligands and mineral partners are part of the reaction system, not background details. The two-organism work shows why measuring oxidation state without checking the dissolved fraction can give an incomplete remediation picture.

limits.text: These results concern chemical immobilization in controlled systems. They do not remove radioactivity or establish long-term performance in a disposal environment. A community that tolerates the experimental exposure has not necessarily evolved a biological requirement for neptunium.

summary.text: Microbes can reduce Pu(V/VI) to particle-associated Pu(IV), yet further reduction can produce soluble Pu(III) when suitable ligands are present. Reduction therefore does not invariably immobilize plutonium.

mechanisms.text: Geobacter metallireducens and Shewanella oneidensis reduced Pu(V/VI) to Pu(IV) in laboratory experiments, producing small cell-associated particles. These observations establish transformation and localization rather than a plutonium nutritional requirement.
With a suitable complexing agent, the same broad class of metal-reducing bacteria can reduce Pu(IV) to Pu(III). Ligand stabilization can keep the product in solution instead of favoring a solid sink.

Microbacterium flavescens accumulated Pu supplied with the siderophore desferrioxamine B. Competition with iron and the dependence on ligand identity linked this uptake to metal-acquisition chemistry.

microbiome.text: The siderophore experiment connects plutonium to machinery usually understood through iron nutrition. It does not show that every iron-scavenging bacterium transports plutonium, or that all siderophores have the same effect. The metal complex presented to the organism is an essential part of the biological result.

exposure.text: A particle-associated Pu(IV) product and a dissolved Pu(III) complex have different transport implications. Describing only total Pu or only whether conditions are “reducing” misses that distinction. The ligand-dependent experiments show why organic complexants must be considered alongside microbial activity.

limits.text: These culture results do not establish disposal performance or human gut uptake. Radioactivity remains, and plutonium-supported growth was not established.

summary.text: Americium research in microbes is mainly about binding and partitioning rather than a demonstrated biological redox cycle. Bacteria, fungal biomass, and dissolved microbial products can change how americium distributes between water, cells, and mineral surfaces.

mechanisms.text: Laboratory work with Escherichia coli and marine bacteria found that americium association depended on the organism and culture conditions. Growth medium and pH are therefore part of the result, not interchangeable technical details.
Rhizopus arrihizus biomass rapidly adsorbed americium from test solutions. This is evidence for a sorbent: accumulation alone does not demonstrate a nutritional role or energy-yielding metabolism.

Immobilizing the fungal biomass improved its handling characteristics and enabled repeated adsorption–desorption experiments. Engineering the physical form of biomass can be as relevant as identifying a binding organism.

microbiome.text: Microbes can also influence the dissolved phase. In the bacterial study, cell-free culture filtrates reduced americium transfer to clay, consistent with microbial products altering partitioning. Thus, a microbe may supply both binding surfaces and compounds that keep metal away from other surfaces.

exposure.text: The fungal experiments tested defined aqueous systems, including acidic conditions. Their adsorption performance cannot be assumed for seawater, mixed waste, or a living host. Immobilization changes how a sorbent can be recovered, but the captured americium remains in the collected material.

limits.text: These studies establish useful laboratory mechanisms, not biological destruction of americium or a proven field cleanup method. A full assessment needs to follow the loaded sorbent, desorption liquids, competing ions, and the stability of retention. High initial capture is only one part of that accounting.

summary.text: Lithium is a light alkali metal included for its value in understanding bacterial ion sensing and tolerance. The most direct evidence here concerns RNA switches and cation export. These mechanisms help cells respond to an unwanted ion; they do not establish lithium as a broadly required microbial nutrient.

mechanisms.text: RNA-based sensing. Two distinct bacterial riboswitch classes were experimentally shown to activate gene expression in response to elevated Li+. They commonly occur beside nhaA transporter genes. The RNA sensor can discriminate a signal that the associated transporter handles less selectively: NhaA transports both lithium and sodium.

Coupling export to the environment. Earlier E. coli work used an nhaA–lacZ reporter to show that both sodium and lithium induce expression. Changing pH alone did not reproduce the ion response, but alkaline conditions increased sensitivity to the ions. Transporter regulation therefore integrates ionic exposure with the acid–base environment.

microbiome.text: These are gene-regulation and culture studies, not trials of prescribed lithium in people. A riboswitch found in an environmental genome indicates a candidate stress-response system. Determining its contribution to a community requires expression and fitness measurements under the local lithium concentration and pH.

exposure.text: The relevant substrate is dissolved Li+, interpreted alongside sodium, pH, and the transporter repertoire. Reporter experiments under defined ion conditions cannot be equated with a medication regimen or a bulk environmental lithium measurement. The response depends on the chemical conditions experienced by the cell.

limits.text: Tolerance, uptake, and nutritional requirement are different claims. The riboswitch work supports protection from lithium toxicity, particularly at high pH; it does not demonstrate a clinical microbiome benefit or a universal community signature.

name: Sodium
role: Broader metal context: sodium gradients, salinity, and gut ecology

summary.text: Sodium belongs to microbial metallomics as an alkali-metal ion with roles in membrane energetics and environmental adaptation. Salt also changes host-associated communities through ecological and host-mediated routes. Sodium gradients, dietary sodium chloride, and circulating microbial metabolites are related but different measurements, and the evidence is clearest when those levels are kept distinct.

mechanisms.text: A respiratory sodium pump. Vibrio cholerae uses Na+-translocating NADH:quinone oxidoreductase, or Na+-NQR, to couple respiration to sodium extrusion. Deleting its encoding genes reduced extrusion and membrane-voltage generation. Cytoplasmic sodium remained broadly similar, illustrating that a maintained concentration can conceal altered flux and energetic cost.

pH makes the gradient consequential. The Na+-NQR mutant had a growth defect under alkaline, low-osmolarity conditions, rescued by restoring the nqr operon. The authors proposed that the pump supplies voltage needed for sodium/proton exchange and cytoplasmic acidification. Thus, adaptation depends on the combination of salinity and pH rather than sodium concentration in isolation.

Salt-responsive gut ecology. In mice, high salt reduced Lactobacillus murinus and altered TH17-related phenotypes. Supplementing the organism modified disease-related outcomes in the mouse experiments. A small human salt challenge also observed changes involving lactobacilli and TH17 cells, but the causal disease experiments were performed in animals.

A human metabolic readout. A randomized crossover sodium-reduction study measured circulating short-chain fatty acids in 145 untreated hypertensive adults. Several increased during sodium reduction, with differences by sex. These are human intervention data on blood metabolites; they do not identify the producing bacterial taxa or demonstrate that microbiome changes caused the blood-pressure response.

microbiome.text: The salt-responsive commensal study joins a mechanistic mouse model to a limited human pilot. The separate crossover trial adds a larger human metabolic observation. Together they support investigating sodium–microbe–host relationships, while leaving a gap between changes in community composition, metabolite production, circulating concentration, and host physiology.

exposure.text: Sodium chloride changes chloride concentration and osmotic conditions as well as sodium availability. The Vibrio experiments manipulated bacterial membrane physiology; dietary interventions changed a host environment. In the crossover trial, serum metabolites also reflected absorption and host handling, so their concentration cannot be read directly as a measure of bacterial production.

limits.text: A high-salt response is not a generic heavy-metal effect. The human pilot does not establish a universal sodium-associated bacterial signature, and the crossover study’s metabolite associations do not prove mediation of cardiovascular effects. Transfer across populations requires attention to background diet, baseline microbiota, and the intervention used.

name: Magnesium
role: Broader metal context: ribosome function and magnesium sensing

summary.text: Magnesium is a major cellular ion that links ribosome stability, energy metabolism, and environmental sensing. Bacteria can monitor magnesium outside the cell through proteins and inside the cell through RNA-based systems. These separate control points help explain why total magnesium is a poor substitute for knowing the available pool at a particular molecular target.

mechanisms.text: An extracellular signal. In Salmonella, magnesium changed the conformation of the periplasmic sensor domain of PhoQ and regulated PhoP-dependent genes. Mutating the sensor changed its response threshold and affected virulence. Magnesium therefore acts both as cellular material and as information about the environment the bacterium occupies.

Ribosomes connect magnesium to phosphate. Low cytoplasmic magnesium destabilized Salmonella ribosomes and slowed protein synthesis. Reduced translation lowered ATP consumption, trapping phosphate in ATP and triggering a phosphate-starvation response despite plentiful external phosphate. Restoration of magnesium balance and ATP consumption ended that response. Apparent starvation can therefore emerge from altered intracellular allocation.

RNA can sense the ion directly. The M-box riboswitch adopts a compact structure in response to divalent metal binding and regulates genes involved in magnesium homeostasis. Structural, genetic, and biochemical experiments established a metal-sensing role for RNA itself, adding a regulatory route alongside protein sensors such as PhoQ.

microbiome.text: The experiments here identify mechanisms in model bacteria, not a predictable community response to magnesium supplementation. They distinguish extracellular sensing, intracellular availability, and downstream metabolic consequences. A community can contain organisms using different sensors and uptake systems; a shared external magnesium concentration need not place them in the same physiological state.

exposure.text: Magnesium added to culture medium, magnesium bound to RNA, and free cytoplasmic magnesium are separate quantities. ATP and ribosomes participate in the intracellular balance. A transcriptomic phosphate-starvation signature, for example, need not mean that environmental phosphate is scarce if translation and ATP turnover have changed.

limits.text: PhoQ findings should not be generalized to organisms that lack the same regulatory system. M-box distribution suggests a broader RNA-based strategy but does not establish identical thresholds or target genes in every lineage. These studies also do not show that host blood magnesium reports the availability encountered by gut bacteria.

name: Potassium
role: Broader metal context: ion homeostasis and biofilm signaling

summary.text: Potassium is a major intracellular ion whose movement can influence both an individual bacterium and its neighbors. In Bacillus subtilis, uptake is regulated by the second messenger cyclic di-AMP, while channel-mediated potassium release supports coordinated biofilm behavior. These are physiological signaling mechanisms demonstrated in laboratory systems, with their wider ecological prevalence still an open question.

mechanisms.text: Metabolic stress becomes a propagating signal. B. subtilis biofilms transmitted potassium waves that changed neighboring cells’ membrane potential. A feedback process linked potassium release to further depolarization and coordinated metabolic states across the community. Deleting the potassium channel abolished the response; altering channel gating hindered propagation.

Uptake is actively restrained. Genetic experiments identified KimA as a potassium importer regulated through a cyclic-di-AMP-responsive RNA element. Higher external potassium was associated with increased cyclic di-AMP. A strain unable to synthesize the messenger could survive at low potassium but not at higher concentrations unless suppressor mutations arose, emphasizing the importance of preventing imbalance.

Signals can extend beyond a biofilm. Microfluidic experiments showed that potassium-mediated electrical activity attracted distant motile cells by influencing membrane potential and movement. Pseudomonas aeruginosa responded to B. subtilis biofilms as well. This demonstrates cross-species interaction under the tested conditions without requiring that both species possess the same dedicated chemical-signal receptor.

microbiome.text: The evidence concerns laboratory biofilms and model-organism genetics. It establishes that ion flux can organize microbial behavior, but it does not establish a response of the human gut microbiota to dietary potassium. Mixed-community relevance will depend on spatial arrangement, flow, available nutrients, ion buffering, and which cells can generate or respond to a signal.

exposure.text: The experiments controlled extracellular potassium and observed uptake, release, or membrane-potential responses. Those fluxes are distinct from total cellular potassium and from dietary intake. In the cyclic-di-AMP study, changing the potassium supply altered whether a genetic defect was lethal, demonstrating that the same regulatory lesion can have different outcomes in different media.

limits.text: A propagating ion signal is a measurable physiological event, not evidence of cognition. Biofilm signaling and potassium import are also different mechanisms: one coordinates neighboring cells, while the other controls cellular accumulation. Demonstrating either in B. subtilis does not establish its prevalence or clinical importance in a host-associated community.

name: Calcium
role: Biofilm architecture, biomineralization, and calcium-responsive signaling

summary.text: Calcium can shape microbial communities as a mineral-building component, a matrix-associated ion, and an environmental signal. Bacillus subtilis and Pseudomonas aeruginosa illustrate different mechanisms. These roles place calcium in broader microbial metallomics, although it is an alkaline-earth metal rather than a heavy metal in conventional usage.

mechanisms.text: A mineral-forming subpopulation. In B. subtilis biofilms, a subset of cells accumulated calcium and initiated calcium carbonate formation. The developing mineral contributed to an organized community scaffold. Inhibiting calcium uptake prevented normal biofilm development under the experimental conditions, linking cellular handling to larger-scale architecture.

Changing the extracellular matrix. In mucoid P. aeruginosa FRD1, calcium addition produced thicker laboratory biofilms and increased alginate-associated gene expression. The extracellular material also contained altered amounts of proteases and other products. Calcium can therefore affect matrix production and composition, not merely serve as an inert bridge between pre-existing polymers.

A defined calcium sensor. P. aeruginosa LadS binds calcium through its periplasmic sensor domain and activates the Gac/Rsm regulatory pathway. Reporter and biochemical experiments linked this response to a shift toward chronic-infection-associated behavior and reduced growth with increased drug tolerance. Clinical isolates retained responsiveness in culture, but the study did not manipulate calcium intake in patients.

microbiome.text: The B. subtilis work examines organized behavior within a bacterial biofilm, while the Pseudomonas studies concern a pathogen and isolates relevant to airway infection. These are community-architecture and cell-regulation findings, not evidence that dietary calcium predictably controls human gut composition. The same ion can participate in distinct structures and signals across organisms.

exposure.text: Dissolved Ca2+, intracellular calcium accumulation, and solid calcium carbonate are different pools. For the mucoid Pseudomonas experiments, calcium chloride was added to defined culture conditions. For biomineralization, formation of a solid phase was part of the biological outcome. Measuring total calcium without resolving these pools can obscure whether the relevant mechanism is sensing, matrix interaction, or mineral formation.

limits.text: The route by which intracellular mineral contributes to the extracellular B. subtilis scaffold was not fully resolved. Pseudomonas calcium responsiveness also depends on the strain and regulatory network. Drug tolerance associated with slower growth in a culture experiment should not be equated with acquisition of a heritable antibiotic-resistance mutation or a measured treatment outcome in patients.

summary.text: Selenium is a nonmetal included because microbial cofactor chemistry, environmental respiration, and host nutrient competition intersect. The chemical form and metabolic role are crucial: selenium incorporated into a protein is different from selenate used as a respiratory electron acceptor. Evidence from cultures and mice supports several such roles without establishing a general benefit from increasing selenium exposure.

mechanisms.text: A respiratory electron acceptor. Thauera selenatis uses a periplasmic selenate reductase that is distinct from its membrane-associated nitrate reductase. Mutants unable to respire nitrate could still grow with selenate. That separation demonstrates a specific selenate-respiration pathway rather than merely an incidental side reaction of nitrate metabolism.

Selenium-containing enzymes in amino-acid fermentation. In C. difficile, growth on paired amino acids used in Stickland metabolism depended on selenium under the tested conditions. Researchers identified glycine- and proline-reductase systems and purified a proline reductase containing a selenocysteine-bearing subunit. Selenium was thus linked to a defined bioenergetic pathway in a gut-associated pathogen.

Host and microbes share a limited resource. Controlled mouse diets altered gut-community composition in selenium-dependent, taxon-specific ways. Comparisons with germ-free and conventionalized animals also found differences in host selenoprotein activity, consistent with microbes capturing part of the available selenium and changing its accessibility to the host.

microbiome.text: The mouse study provides bidirectional evidence: dietary selenium influenced community composition, and colonization influenced host selenium responses. Different phylotypes responded differently, even within a genus. The C. difficile culture work adds a specific metabolic mechanism but does not show that this organism accounts for the dietary-community result or that selenium intake determines infection in humans.

exposure.text: Selenate, selenite, and organic selenium compounds should be identified separately when interpreting an exposure. The environmental respiration study used selenate as an electron acceptor, while the host study manipulated dietary selenium availability. Protein-bound selenium reflects incorporation into a cofactor-bearing enzyme, not the same pool as dissolved selenium undergoing environmental reduction.

limits.text: A pathogen’s selenium-dependent growth pathway is not a reason to infer that all selenium is detrimental to a community. Conversely, increased diversity in a mouse dietary experiment is not proof of improved human health. The consequences depend on the organisms, substrates, chemical forms, and host demands involved, and the cited studies do not establish a clinical microbiome intervention.

summary.text: Rubidium is useful for understanding how bacteria distinguish chemically similar alkali-metal ions. It can enter through potassium-handling systems and can partly substitute for potassium under some culture conditions. Transportability, however, is not the same as physiological equivalence: the transporter, strain, and potassium background change the result.

mechanisms.text: Entry through Kup. Experiments with E. coli identified Kup, formerly called TrkD, as a potassium-uptake system with relatively limited discrimination among potassium, rubidium, and cesium. The result establishes a route by which a chemically similar ion can enter a cell without a dedicated rubidium-specific nutritional pathway.

Different transporters discriminate differently. Earlier E. coli work compared potassium transport systems using rubidium tracer measurements. The high-affinity Kdp system strongly discriminated against rubidium, while other systems showed different selectivities. A rubidium-based uptake assay can therefore misrepresent potassium flux if transporter identity is ignored.

Substitution is conditional. A later study of E. coli alkali-ion transport included rubidium as a comparator and observed support of growth in potassium-depleted medium. Earlier work found that rubidium met only part of the potassium requirement and produced poorer growth than potassium. These observations should be read with their strains, media, residual potassium, and endpoints attached.

microbiome.text: The evidence here is bacterial transport and growth in defined media. It does not describe a rubidium-associated human gut community or demonstrate that rubidium availability controls host physiology through microbes. Its immediate value is mechanistic and methodological: similar ions can enter the same pathway yet differ in the functions they sustain.

exposure.text: Relevant measurements include dissolved rubidium, competing potassium, transporter expression, and residual potassium in nominally depleted medium. In the later culture study, background potassium was measured, emphasizing why an apparent substitution experiment must account for the ion being replaced.

limits.text: Rubidium should not automatically be treated as a faithful potassium tracer. Nor does short-term growth in a supplemented culture establish a universal requirement or long-term replacement of potassium. Differences between transport assays and growth assays are informative: uptake tests passage through a membrane, whereas growth integrates many intracellular functions.
